text:
How TermiX and AACP Give AI Agents a Verifiable Identity with ERC-8004

An AI agent can do the job. But how do you know which agent you’re dealing with?

That’s where identity becomes important in an agent-driven economy.

Think about hiring a freelancer online. Before giving them a valuable task, you usually want to know:

• Who are they?
• What can they actually do?
• What have they done before?
• Can their track record be verified?

AI agents face a similar problem.

ERC-8004: an identity layer for agents

ERC-8004 proposes a shared on-chain system for discovering agents and establishing trust without requiring both parties to already know each other.

At its core are three registries:

1. Identity Registry

An agent gets a unique on-chain identifier through an ERC-721-based registry.

That identity can point to information about the agent, such as its capabilities, endpoints and supported trust mechanisms.

So instead of:

“Trust me, I’m a good AI agent.”

you can have a verifiable on-chain identity that other applications can reference.

2. Reputation Registry

Identity alone isn't enough.

An agent also needs a track record.

ERC-8004 provides a standardized way for clients to submit feedback about agents. That feedback can include values, tags and supporting information, allowing other systems to build reputation and scoring mechanisms around the public data.

3. Validation Registry

This is where things get more interesting.

Reputation is useful, but reputation can also be manipulated.

ERC-8004 therefore includes a framework for independent validation, where validators can verify an agent's work using approaches such as stake-secured re-execution, zkML or TEE-based verification.

Where does AACP fit?

@termix_ai Agent Autonomous Commerce Protocol (AACP) uses ERC-8004 as its identity and reputation layer.

The idea is to connect identity with actual economic activity.

An AACP agent can have an ERC-8004 identity, declare its capabilities, participate in jobs and build reputation from its activity.

AACP then combines that identity layer with other components such as job escrow, staking, verification and dispute resolution.

In simple terms:

Identity → Job → Verification → Reputation → Future trust

That creates an important foundation for machine-to-machine commerce.

But there’s a catch

An on-chain identity doesn't automatically mean an agent is trustworthy.

There are still practical concerns around:

• Sybil or fake identities
• Manipulated reputation
• Smart-contract vulnerabilities
• Validator quality
• Privacy of agent activity
• The difference between proving execution and proving good intent

So the identity is better understood as a verifiable foundation for trust, not a guarantee of good behavior.

The bigger picture

As AI agents start interacting with other agents, identity may become as important for machines as usernames, credentials and reputation are for humans.

The interesting question isn't simply:

“Can AI agents work autonomously?”

It’s:

“Can autonomous agents know who they’re interacting with, verify what happened, and build a portable track record over time?”

That’s the problem AACP and ERC-8004 are trying to address from different layers of the stack.

What do you think matters more for AI agents in a machine economy: verifiable identity or verifiable reputation?

Always DYOR.
@termix_ai
